claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 has a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation.
(MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 has poor structural integrity and tends to crack.
A minor boron source with trace Hf and Mo will promote in-situ formation of high-entropy boride nanoprecipitates at approximately 5 vol%.
The boride nanoprecipitates will be nanoscale, coherent, and uniformly dispersed in the matrix.
The boride nanoprecipitates will act as crack-deflection and crack-arrest sites.
Hard secondary-phase precipitates can reinforce an alloy matrix.
The proposed boride nanoprecipitates will retard crack initiation.
The proposed boride nanoprecipitates will retard crack propagation.
The nanoprecipitate intervention will preserve the phase transition responsible for the caloric effect.
The modified alloy will attain a compressive strength greater than 200 MPa.
The modified alloy will have greater ductility than the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will retain a caloric-response magnitude comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
The predicted behavior will hold under the same applied-field, pressure-field, temperature, and loading regimes used for the unmodified alloy.
Excessive precipitate volume fraction or precipitate growth can deteriorate mechanical performance.
Excessive or nonuniform boride precipitation may cause mechanical embrittlement.
Excessive precipitation or altered phase equilibrium may diminish the caloric response.
The optimal precipitate volume fraction and distribution are not known and require experimental calibration.
Failure to improve mechanical integrity or notable degradation of caloric response would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The modified sample is described as receiving boron plus trace Hf/Mo, but the experiment subsequently says all variables are identical except for boron addition. Hf and Mo would be additional changed variables unless separately controlled.
